notes.meaning: God speaks directly to Ezekiel to give him a fresh message. Ezekiel receives this divine word while living in exile by the river, showing that the Lord has not forgotten His people. The prophet must deliver this warning even though he is far from the land of Israel.

The Lord tells Ezekiel to face toward the mountains of Israel and preach against them. These hills were the political heartland of the nation and the main spots where people built altars to false gods. Speaking directly to the silent mountains also highlights how stubborn the people were, because the rocks would hear God's word better than the rebels would.

Ezekiel calls out to the hills, ravines, and valleys to hear the Lord's warning of war. Idolatry—the worship of false gods—had spread into every valley and hilltop across the land. God announces that He will bring foreign armies to destroy all the pagan shrines built upon the high places.

The pagan altars and sun images will be completely smashed to pieces. God warns that the dead bodies of the worshipers will fall right in front of the statues they trusted. These powerless idols will stand by helplessly as their own followers perish before them.

God declares that human corpses and bones will be scattered around the pagan altars. Under biblical law, dead bodies defiled holy places and made them completely unclean. This grim scene would ruin the shrines forever and prove that the false gods could never save their followers.

The coming destruction will reach beyond the hills into every town where the people live. Cities will become ruins, and every idol carved by human hands will be wiped out. God will tear down all the religious works that human beings created in place of true worship.

As casualties fall across the cities and countryside, the survivors will finally recognize the Lord. This is the first time Ezekiel uses the phrase, 'you will know that I am the LORD,' which becomes a major theme of his book. When false hopes collapse, people are brought face-to-face with the reality of God's power.

God promises that He will not destroy the entire nation, but will spare a remnant. A remnant is a small surviving group that God preserves to carry forward His covenant promises. Even though they will be scattered into foreign lands as captives, God's mercy will keep them alive.

In foreign nations, the surviving captives will finally remember the Lord and turn back to Him. God explains that their unfaithfulness broke His heart, just as an unfaithful spouse breaks the heart of a loving partner. When the people see the harm they caused, they will feel deep sorrow and loathe their evil deeds.

The survivors will realize that the Lord is the one true God and that His warnings were never empty threats. The people had ignored the prophets for years, but the disaster proved that God keeps His word. True repentance leads people to admit that God's judgments are entirely right.

God commands Ezekiel to clap his hands, stomp his feet, and cry out in distress over Israel's evil deeds. These forceful actions showed deep shock and grief over the horrors coming upon the land. The nation faced a deadly threefold punishment of war, famine, and sickness.

No one will escape God's judgment, no matter where they try to hide. Those far away will fall to disease, those nearby will die in battle, and those trapped in besieged cities will starve. In this way, God will carry out His holy anger against unfaithfulness.

Slain bodies will lie beside the ruined altars under every green hill and leafy tree where people once burned sweet-smelling incense to idols. The foul smell of death where pleasant fragrances once rose will expose the total emptiness of false gods. Through this tragedy, the people will finally see that the Lord alone is God.

God will reach out His mighty hand against the people and leave the entire country as an empty wilderness. The judgment will cover the whole land, from the southern desert to Diblah. When the devastation is complete, the people will finally acknowledge that the Lord is God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that ancient scribes likely wrote 'Diblah' by mistake for 'Riblah,' since the Hebrew letters look almost identical. Reading Riblah describes the land from the southern desert all the way to Riblah in the far north.
